nullPointer.title: Possible null pointer dereference
nullPointer.summary: A pointer that might be null is being dereferenced.
nullPointer.why: Dereferencing a null pointer leads to immediate program crashes (segmentation faults). This usually happens when a pointer is returned from a function that can fail, and the caller forgets to check if it's null before using it.
nullPointer.exampleBefore:
int* ptr = getResource();
*ptr = 5; // Dangerous if ptr is null
notes: Always check pointers returned by functions for null before dereferencing.
Consider using references instead of pointers if null is not a valid state.

memleak.title: Memory leak
memleak.summary: Dynamically allocated memory is never freed.
memleak.why: Failing to release dynamically allocated memory causes the program to consume increasing amounts of RAM over time. In long-running applications, this will eventually exhaust system memory and crash.
notes: Avoid raw pointers for memory management. Use smart pointers like std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr.

uninitvar.title: Uninitialized variable
uninitvar.summary: A variable is used before it is assigned a value.
uninitvar.why: Reading from an uninitialized variable yields garbage data left over in memory. This results in unpredictable behavior and non-deterministic bugs that are incredibly hard to track down.
notes: Always initialize variables at the point of declaration.

outOfBounds.title: Array index out of bounds
outOfBounds.summary: An attempt to access an array element outside its valid range.
outOfBounds.why: Accessing memory outside the bounds of an array corrupts adjacent memory or causes a segmentation fault. This is a severe security vulnerability that can be exploited by attackers.
notes: Prefer std::vector or std::array over raw C-style arrays.
Use range-based for loops to prevent off-by-one errors.

useClosedFile.title: Using a closed file
useClosedFile.summary: A file handle is being used after it has been closed.
useClosedFile.why: Once a file handle is closed, the operating system reclaims the resource. Attempting to read from or write to a closed file handle will fail and may corrupt other open files if the handle was reassigned.
notes: Prefer C++ file streams (std::ifstream, std::ofstream) as their destructors automatically close the file safely.

resourceLeak.title: Resource leak
resourceLeak.summary: A system resource (like a file handle or network socket) is acquired but not released.
resourceLeak.why: Similar to memory leaks, failing to release system resources can lead to exhaustion, preventing the application or even the entire OS from opening new files or connections.
notes: Use RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) to manage all resources automatically.

syntaxError.title: Syntax Error / Unparsable code
syntaxError.summary: Cppcheck could not parse the code due to invalid syntax or complex macros.
syntaxError.why: If the code is unparsable, the static analysis tool cannot guarantee the safety or correctness of the file. This often happens with heavily macro-obfuscated code.
notes: Ensure your code compiles successfully. If macros are causing the issue, try to simplify them or configure cppcheck to ignore them.
